paras: The killing of John Anderson at Cokato took place on October 6, 1888, when James Erickson struck Anderson, a farmer, two blows in a saloon at Cokato, Minnesota, and Anderson died almost instantly. Erickson was arrested, released on bail, and indicted by a Wright County grand jury in December. One St. Paul paper added that Erickson had "barely escaped lynching at the time," a claim no other report repeated.

The New Ulm Weekly Review placed the encounter in one of the town's saloons at the close of the Cokato monthly fair, and identified Erickson as a saloon keeper of Annandale and Anderson as "a well-known farmer of French Lake township." The St. Paul Daily Globe instead called Erickson "of Cokato" and said Anderson was a stranger to him.

Accounts of how the quarrel began differ. According to the Globe, Erickson was "drunk and very pugnacious" and ordered Anderson, who was talking to a friend, to shut up with an oath before hitting him. The New Ulm paper said Anderson came in "in an inebriated condition," argued with the bartender over the price of drinks, and was struck after objecting to insulting remarks from Erickson. Both agreed that Erickson struck two blows, the second to the stomach, and that Anderson died almost at once.

Erickson was arrested immediately and taken to Buffalo, where Sheriff Nugent held him. The Globe's report closed with the single sentence that Erickson "barely escaped lynching at the time," giving no account of who threatened him or how he escaped.

On October 16 Erickson appeared in district court to have his bond fixed, six "well-known citizens" stood as his sureties, and he was set at liberty. He engaged the St. Paul criminal lawyer Erwin, who the Globe expected to "spring some unique defense." In December the grand jury at Buffalo returned an indictment against "Erickson of Annandale" for the killing, naming the dead man as "Johnson." No report of the trial or its outcome was found.

Coverage came entirely from the white press of Minnesota and Dakota, and most of it was brief. The Swedish-language Skaffaren of St. Paul reported the death under the heading "Dräpslag" (manslaughter) on October 10, and the Sauk Centre Herald gave it one line among state news notes. A longer "fatal saloon row" paragraph ran in the New Ulm Weekly Review under "Man's Wicked Doings" and was reprinted the same week in Minnesota, South Dakota and North Dakota weeklies, while the Pembina Pioneer Express filed a shorter version under "Petty Criminalities."

Only the St. Paul Daily Globe, under the headline "CHARGED WITH MURDER," took a moral tone, calling Erickson "the burly murderer" and noting that Anderson "left a family without means of support." It was also the only paper to mention a lynching, and it did so in passing, without comment. When it reported his release on bail, Skaffaren called Erickson "den mera nämde" (the much-mentioned) man accused of murder at Cokato.

reader.title: Killing of John Anderson at Cokato
bases: The papers describe a one-on-one saloon killing of John Anderson by James Erickson (A1, A3, A5); the only mob element is one unelaborated sentence in A3 saying Erickson 'barely escaped lynching at the time', with no account of any crowd, threat or act.

No one was killed by a group: Anderson died from blows struck by one man in a saloon fight (A3, A5), and the alleged near-lynching of Erickson rests on a single sentence in A3 that names no mob, size or act; Erickson survived, was jailed, bailed and indicted (A5, A3, A11).

The saloon killing itself is reported independently by several papers (A1, A2, A3, A5), but the lynching threat that brings it into scope appears only in the St. Paul Globe (A3) and in none of the other reports.

accounts.label: Minnesota news-service paragraph
accounts.gist: Anderson, inebriated, disputed drink prices with the bartender; Erickson made insulting remarks, and when Anderson objected to his tone struck him in the neck and stomach; Erickson was arrested at once. No mob is mentioned.

framing.detail: Minnesota and Dakota weeklies carried the killing as a one-line item or a 'fatal saloon row' paragraph in crime columns such as 'Petty Criminalities' and 'Man's Wicked Doings'.
The St. Paul Globe, under 'CHARGED WITH MURDER', called Erickson 'the burly murderer' and stressed the destitute family, and mentioned the near-lynching without comment.

conflicts.note: Every October report names Anderson; the December indictment brief alone says Johnson, likely an error.

John Anderson, a farmer of French Lake township, killed by blows from James Erickson; Erickson himself was the man said to have 'barely escaped lynching'
Erickson was charged with the murder of Anderson and later indicted for killing him
Of the killing: James Erickson, alone. Of the alleged near-lynching: not described
